Plug-in solar: the practical guide

Since 27 August 2026 you can buy a small solar kit in England, Scotland and Wales, plug it into a socket and use the power at home. Here is what the rules say, how to mount the panels safely, and what to expect on your bill.

Check your set-up with the planner

What plug-in solar is

A plug-in kit is one to four solar panels with a small inverter and a plug. The inverter turns the panels' power into mains electricity and feeds it into your home's wiring through a normal socket. Anything switched on at home uses the solar power first, and only the shortfall comes from the grid. The kits switch off automatically in a power cut.

In Germany these kits have been common for years, where they are called Balkonkraftwerk, “balcony power station”. Around 1.5 million were registered there by September 2026. Northern Ireland is not covered by the new rules yet.

The rules for the kit

  • 800 VA maximum: the inverter may feed in no more than 800 VA. The panels may add up to 2,000 W across up to four panels, with no more than two in series. Bigger panels do not lift the 800 VA limit, they just produce more in weak light.
  • Only complete, listed kits: the whole kit has to meet the official product specification and be listed on the Energy Networks Association's type test register (G98). Buy only from retailers who show this.
  • Moulded plug: the kit comes with a factory-fitted, non-rewirable UK plug fused at 5 A or less.
  • One kit per home: kits must not be daisy-chained or plugged into several sockets.
  • Register it: register the kit within 28 days of plugging it in, through the official registration site (myplugin.solar).
  • No batteries yet: plug-in batteries are not covered by the new rules. A battery has to be wired in permanently by a qualified electrician.

The socket and your wiring

  • Wall socket only: plug the kit straight into a fixed wall socket. Extension leads and multi-socket adaptors are not allowed, as they can overheat.
  • Outdoor socket: if the plug is outside, you need a weatherproof outdoor socket. Consumer guides put the cost at around £140 to £260 if you have one fitted.
  • Check older wiring: have an electrician check your wiring before you start (an EICR, roughly £100 to £250) and tell them you plan to add plug-in solar. The circuit should be protected by an RCD or RCBO.
  • Cable length: make sure the kit's cable reaches the socket. Only use extension cables made for solar (MC4) and check they are safe.

Where the panels work best

Facing south and unshaded is best. East or west still works, with less power in the evening or morning. North-facing spots get too little sun. A tilt of about 30 to 35 degrees gives the most over the year. Panels hung vertically on a wall or railing produce noticeably less. Even small shadows from a tree or railing can cut the output a lot, so watch the spot over a sunny day before you buy.

For today's kits the garden is usually the best place. Panels are big: a 400 W panel measures about 1.8 × 1.2 m and can weigh up to 20 kg, so measure the space carefully.

Planning rules in England

Most installations are permitted development, as long as they stay within these limits:

  • In the garden: no more than 9 m² of panels. Maximum height 1 m within 5 m of the boundary in front of the house, 2 m within 5 m of the boundary elsewhere, 2 m in a conservation area closer to the road than the house, and 4 m anywhere else.
  • On a wall or balcony: sticking out no more than 0.4 m, or 0.2 m if the wall faces a road.
  • On a flat roof: no more than 0.6 m above the highest part of the roof.
  • No timber: not on a wooden fence, gate, wall or balcony, or on timber cladding.
  • Special places: listed buildings need consent. In conservation areas, National Parks, National Landscapes, the Broads and World Heritage Sites, panels within 5 m of the boundary need prior approval. Flats have stricter rules.

The plug-in solar planner works out the height and projection from your panel size and tilt and checks them against these limits.

Mounting safely: lessons from 1.5 million German kits

German consumer advice puts a lot of weight on mounting: the panel must not be damaged or loosened by wind or fall under its own weight. A tilted panel works like a sail, and stands are the most exposed, because a gust can slide them, tip them over or lift them. These are the points that matter, from the German experience and the UK kit rules:

  • Secure every stand: stands on the ground or on a flat roof need ballast or fixings. In Germany, paving slabs are the usual ballast for garden stands. Screwing the stand to a solid base is better still.
  • Use proper fixings: under the UK rules, mounting held only by cable ties, rope, tape, bungee cords or straps is not allowed. Fixings have to be removable and must not damage the building's structure, fire protection or weatherproofing.
  • Follow the manufacturer: use the mounting system made for your panels. Drilling extra holes in the panel frame can weaken it and void the warranty.
  • Not on a shared wall: panels may not be fixed to a wall that separates your home from a neighbour's.
  • Protect the cable: route the cable so nobody trips over it and it cannot be pinched in a window or door.

Fixing to a masonry wall

This is where a mason's advice helps. Fix brackets into the brick or block itself, not into the mortar joints, which are weaker. The right fixing depends on the wall:

  • Solid brick and concrete: nylon plugs or heavy-duty anchors of the size the bracket maker specifies.
  • Perforated bricks: resin anchors with a mesh sleeve, because normal plugs find nothing to grip in the holes.
  • Aerated concrete blocks: special anchors for aerated concrete. Normal plugs pull out easily.
  • Rendered or insulated walls: the fixing has to reach through the render or insulation into the solid wall. Seal the holes so that no water gets in.

If you are not sure what your wall is made of, drill a small test hole in an inconspicuous spot and look at the dust: red dust means brick, grey means concrete or block, and white means aerated block or plaster.

Renting, flats and insurance

Tenants need their landlord's permission to fix panels anywhere in or around the home, and flat owners need the freeholder's or managing agent's. Ask before you buy. In blocks of flats, fire safety comes first, especially where cladding has been an issue. Tell your home insurer before you install a kit.

What it costs and saves

Compliant kits cost from around £450. The government expects savings of about £70 to £110 a year. The Energy Saving Trust estimates that an 800 W kit produces about 700 kWh a year (facing south at 30°, in Manchester) and saves about £100 a year if someone is at home during the day, or £70 if the home is empty all day. Which? puts the payback at about 3.6 to 7.1 years.

The saving comes from not buying electricity, not from selling it. Fridges, freezers and other devices that are always on use most of the solar power. Some suppliers pay for exported power, but the amounts are small. If the kit, an outdoor socket and a wiring check together cost £1,000 or more, it takes much longer to pay back.

Mistakes to avoid

  • Buying a kit that is not on the type test register.
  • Using a normal extension lead or adaptor.
  • Skipping the wiring check in an older home.
  • Expecting more than 800 VA from a bigger kit.
  • Fixing panels to a wooden fence, gate or balcony.
  • Leaving stands unsecured in the wind.
  • Forgetting to register within 28 days or to ask the landlord first.

Frequently asked questions

Is plug-in solar legal in the UK?
Yes, in England, Scotland and Wales since 27 August 2026, for certified complete kits of up to 800 VA. Northern Ireland is not covered yet.
How much does plug-in solar save?
Usually about £70 to £110 a year, depending on how much of the solar power you use during the day. An 800 W kit produces roughly 700 kWh a year in a good spot.
Can I use an extension lead?
No. The kit must go straight into a fixed wall socket. Extension leads and adaptors can overheat and are not allowed.
Can I put plug-in solar on my balcony?
On a masonry or metal balcony, often yes, if the landlord or freeholder agrees. On a house in England the panels may stick out no more than 0.4 m. Never on a wooden balcony. Gardens usually give more power.
Do I need to tell anyone?
Register the kit within 28 days, tell your home insurer, and get permission from your landlord or freeholder if you do not own the building.

All timber sections are guide values and do not replace a structural calculation. Carports and patio covers may need planning permission and building regulations approval, and a structural engineer's check depending on where you live.
